title: Graph Traversal
notes: Diagram-heavy: the lecture describes small ASCII graphs and queue/stack traces. The summary must keep BFS-queue and DFS-stack pairing straight. Traps: shortest-path and spanning-tree algorithms that follow in most courses but are not in this lecture.

pages.text:
Week 6 — Graph Traversal.

A graph has vertices and edges. We store it as an adjacency list: for each vertex, the list of its neighbours. Memory use is proportional to vertices plus edges.

    A --- B
    |     |
    C --- D

Breadth-first search (BFS) uses a queue. Start at A: queue [A]. Visit A, enqueue B and C. Visit B, enqueue D. Order: A B C D. BFS visits vertices in order of distance from the start, so in an unweighted graph it finds the fewest-edge path.

Depth-first search (DFS) uses a stack, or recursion. Start at A: go to B, then D, then C. Order: A B D C. DFS goes as deep as possible before backing up.
Both mark vertices as visited so a cycle cannot cause an infinite loop. Both run in O(V + E) with an adjacency list.
